mean: to stay up late into the night to work or study
lit: to drive the night train: keep going through the hours when everyone else is asleep

use.how: A verb-object phrase that can be split: 开夜车, 开了几个夜车, 又开夜车. Said of working or studying late to meet a deadline, never of partying.

near.diff: 熬夜 is any staying up late, for any reason; 开夜车 is staying up specifically to get work or study done.
夜猫子 is a noun for a person who habitually stays up late; 开夜车 is a verb phrase for one late night of work.

cue: Your report is due at nine tomorrow morning and you have not started it, so you will be at your desk until three a.m. What are you doing tonight?

ctx.s: 明天就考试了，我今天晚上得{开夜车}了。
ctx.en: The exam is tomorrow, so I'll have to stay up late studying tonight.

ctx.s: 你眼睛这么红，昨天又{开夜车}了吧？
ctx.en: Your eyes are so red, you were up working late again last night, weren't you?

ctx.s: 为了赶这个项目，他连着三天{开夜车}。
ctx.en: To get this project done in time, he worked late into the night three days running.

ctx.s: 论文截止前一周，宿舍里几乎人人都在{开夜车}。
ctx.en: In the week before the thesis deadline, almost everyone in the dorm was studying late into the night.

ctx.s: 妈妈劝他：“别老{开夜车}，身体要紧。”
ctx.en: His mum urged him: "Don't keep working late into the night, your health comes first."

ctx.s: 上周我{开了好几个夜车}，总算把报告写完了。
ctx.en: Last week I stayed up late working several nights and finally finished the report.

bad.s: 他是个{开夜车}，每天都很晚才睡。
bad.en: (meant: he's a night owl who always goes to bed late)
bad.why: It is a verb phrase for working late on a task, not a noun for a person; a habitual late sleeper is a ye mao zi (night owl).

bad.s: 昨晚我们去酒吧{开夜车}，一直玩到半夜。
bad.en: (meant: last night we went to a bar and partied until midnight)
bad.why: It means staying up to work or study; staying out late to have fun is not this.

mean: to fire someone from their job
lit: to stir-fry squid: the squid pieces curl up into rolls in the hot pan

story.text: The expression comes from Cantonese. In the past a worker who was dismissed rolled up his bedding and left, so being sacked was called rolling up one's bedding. Squid pieces curl into tight rolls when stir-fried, so a fried squid came to stand for the rolled-up bedding of a dismissed worker. The phrase spread from Guangdong and Hong Kong to the rest of China.

use.how: A verb-object phrase, mostly passive (被炒鱿鱼) or split around the person: 炒了他的鱿鱼. Informal; official texts use 开除 or 解聘.

near.diff: 开除 is the formal word and also covers expelling a student or a member; 炒鱿鱼 is casual and only about losing a job.
跳槽 is leaving by choice for another employer; 炒鱿鱼 is being sent away by the employer.

cue: Your friend kept coming in late, and yesterday the manager told him to clear his desk and not come back. What happened to him?

ctx.s: 他上班老迟到，结果被老板{炒鱿鱼}了。
ctx.en: He was always late for work, and in the end the boss fired him.

ctx.s: 你再这样偷懒，小心被{炒鱿鱼}！
ctx.en: If you keep slacking off like this, watch out or you'll get the sack!

ctx.s: 经理一气之下，当场{炒了他的鱿鱼}。
ctx.en: In a fit of anger, the manager fired him on the spot.

ctx.s: 听说公司要裁员，大家都怕自己被{炒鱿鱼}。
ctx.en: Word is the company is cutting staff, and everyone is afraid of being let go.

ctx.s: 与其等着被{炒鱿鱼}，不如自己先辞职。
ctx.en: Rather than wait to be fired, you'd better resign first.

ctx.s: 这个老板脾气很怪，一个月就{炒了三个员工的鱿鱼}。
ctx.en: This boss has a strange temper; he fired three employees in a single month.

bad.s: 学校把那个考试作弊的学生{炒鱿鱼}了。
bad.en: (meant: the school expelled the student who cheated in the exam)
bad.why: It is only about losing a job. Expelling a student is kai chu.

bad.s: 公司公告：经研究决定，对张某予以{炒鱿鱼}处理。
bad.en: (meant: company notice: after review, it has been decided to dismiss Zhang)
bad.why: It is slang and cannot appear in an official notice; a formal text uses kai chu or jie pin (dismiss).

mean: to flatter someone in power to win their favour
lit: to pat a horse on the rump

use.how: A verb-object phrase; the person flattered goes in the middle: 拍领导的马屁, 别拍我马屁. Said disapprovingly of insincere praise aimed upward.

near.diff: 讨好 is trying to please anyone, a child or a friend included, by any means; 拍马屁 is crude flattery of someone above you.
吹牛 is boasting about yourself; 拍马屁 is praising someone else to get something from them.

cue: A new employee laughs loudly at every joke the boss makes and praises his tie every morning, hoping for a promotion. What is he doing?

ctx.s: 他就会{拍马屁}，真本事一点儿也没有。
ctx.en: All he's good at is sucking up; he has no real ability at all.

ctx.s: 你别{拍我马屁}了，有什么事直说吧。
ctx.en: Stop buttering me up. If you want something, just say it.

ctx.s: 我说的是真心话，不是{拍马屁}。
ctx.en: I really mean it, I'm not just flattering you.

ctx.s: 他天天{拍经理的马屁}，就是想早点升职。
ctx.en: He sucks up to the manager every day just so he can get promoted sooner.

ctx.s: 整天夸领导、{拍马屁}，在我们公司是升不了职的。
ctx.en: Praising the boss all day and sucking up won't get you promoted at our company.

ctx.s: 会上几个人轮流{拍领导的马屁}，谁也不提问题。
ctx.en: At the meeting several people took turns flattering the boss, and nobody raised any problems.

bad.s: 老师今天{拍了我的马屁}，说我的作文写得很好。
bad.en: (meant: today the teacher praised me, saying my essay was very good)
bad.why: It is self-serving flattery of someone more powerful, said with contempt; a teacher's honest praise is biao yang.

bad.s: 他很会{拍马屁}领导，所以升得很快。
bad.en: (meant: he is good at flattering the boss, so he rose quickly)
bad.why: It takes no object after it; the person goes inside the phrase: pai lingdao de mapi.

mean: to brag or talk big about oneself
lit: to blow up an ox: puff air into an oxhide until it swells (short for chui niu pi)

use.how: A verb-object phrase with no object of its own; it can be split: 吹什么牛, 吹了一晚上的牛. Often teasing among friends: 别吹牛了。

near.diff: 拍马屁 is praising someone powerful to win favour; 吹牛 is exaggerating your own abilities or deeds.
打包票 is guaranteeing a result, which may be sincere; 吹牛 is boastful talk that others doubt.

cue: Your friend claims he once beat a national table-tennis champion and can drink ten beers without feeling a thing. What is he doing?

ctx.s: 别{吹牛}了，你哪会说五种语言？
ctx.en: Stop bragging. Since when can you speak five languages?

ctx.s: 我不是{吹牛}，这道菜我做得比饭店还好吃。
ctx.en: I'm not boasting, but I make this dish better than any restaurant.

ctx.s: 他喝了点儿酒就开始{吹牛}，说自己认识很多明星。
ctx.en: After a few drinks he starts talking big, saying he knows lots of celebrities.

ctx.s: 你{吹什么牛}啊，上次比赛你不是输了吗？
ctx.en: What are you bragging about? Didn't you lose the last match?

ctx.s: 几个老同学坐在一起，{吹了一晚上的牛}。
ctx.en: A few old classmates sat together and spent the whole evening talking big.

ctx.s: 他在网上总爱{吹牛}，其实生活很普通。
ctx.en: Online he loves to brag, but in fact his life is very ordinary.

bad.s: 你考了第一名，太{吹牛}了！
bad.en: (meant: you came first, that's awesome!)
bad.why: 'Awesome' is tai niu le. This idiom is a verb meaning to brag and cannot be used as an adjective of praise.

bad.s: 他总是{吹牛}老板，说老板特别英明。
bad.en: (meant: he always flatters the boss, saying how wise he is)
bad.why: It is boasting about oneself and takes no person as object; flattering the boss is pai mapi.

mean: to get something done through connections, not proper channels
lit: to go in by the back door instead of the front entrance

use.how: A verb-object phrase, often after 靠 or 通过, or split: 走了他舅舅的后门, 走个后门. Said of jobs, school places, permits or tickets gained unfairly.

near.diff: 开绿灯 is what the person in charge does in letting something through; 走后门 is what the person seeking the favour does.
拉关系 is building up useful connections; 走后门 is actually using them to get around the rules.

cue: The hospital waiting list is three months long, but your neighbour's cousin knows the director and got an appointment for tomorrow. How did he get it?

ctx.s: 听说他的工作是{走后门}找到的。
ctx.en: I heard he got his job through connections.

ctx.s: 这件事按规定办，谁也别想{走后门}。
ctx.en: This will be handled by the rules; nobody should expect to pull strings.

ctx.s: 他{走了舅舅的后门}，才进了这家银行。
ctx.en: It was only through his uncle's connections that he got into this bank.

ctx.s: 你在医院有熟人吗？能不能帮我{走个后门}？
ctx.en: Do you know anyone at the hospital? Could you pull a few strings for me?

ctx.s: 我们要凭考试成绩进名校，不能靠{走后门}。
ctx.en: We should get into a top school on our exam results, not through connections.

ctx.s: 招聘改成公开考试以后，想{走后门}的人少多了。
ctx.en: Since hiring switched to open exams, far fewer people try to get in through the back door.

bad.s: 他靠自己的努力{走后门}，终于考上了大学。
bad.en: (meant: through his own hard work he finally got into university)
bad.why: It means bypassing the rules through connections; it is never earned by effort and is never praise.

bad.s: 我们公司上个月{走后门}了一个大客户。
bad.en: (meant: last month our company landed a big client through networking)
bad.why: It cannot take an object, and it implies getting around rules or queues, not ordinary business networking.

mean: to stand someone up after making plans with them

use.how: A verb-object phrase; the person let down goes in the middle (放我鸽子, 放了他的鸽子) or it is passive (被放鸽子). Said of failing to turn up as agreed.

near.diff: 爽约 is the neutral, more written word for breaking an appointment; 放鸽子 is casual and carries the speaker's annoyance.

cue: You booked a table for two at seven and waited an hour, but your friend never showed up and never called. What did he do to you?

ctx.s: 说好六点见面，他又{放我鸽子}了。
ctx.en: We agreed to meet at six, and he stood me up again.

ctx.s: 你明天可一定要来，别{放我鸽子}啊！
ctx.en: You really must come tomorrow, don't stand me up!

ctx.s: 我被客户{放了鸽子}，在咖啡馆白等了一个小时。
ctx.en: The client stood me up, and I waited in the café for an hour for nothing.

ctx.s: 他答应来参加聚会，结果{放了大家的鸽子}。
ctx.en: He promised to come to the party, but in the end he let everyone down and didn't show.

ctx.s: 这已经是她第三次{放鸽子}了，我再也不信她了。
ctx.en: That's the third time she's failed to show up; I'll never believe her again.

ctx.s: 那位歌手临时取消演出，{放了几万名观众的鸽子}。
ctx.en: The singer cancelled the concert at the last minute, leaving tens of thousands of fans in the lurch.

bad.s: 她{放了我的鸽子}，跟我分手了。
bad.en: (meant: she dumped me and broke up with me)
bad.why: It means failing to turn up for an arranged meeting, not ending a relationship; being dumped is bei shuai le.

bad.s: 昨天我{放鸽子}了他，现在很后悔。
bad.en: (meant: yesterday I stood him up, and now I regret it)
bad.why: The person cannot follow the phrase; it goes inside it: fang le ta de gezi, or fang ta gezi.

mean: to feel jealous over a romantic partner
lit: to eat vinegar: the sour taste of jealousy

story.text: The story usually told to explain it: Emperor Taizong of Tang wanted to give his chancellor Fang Xuanling some concubines, but Fang's wife would not allow it. The emperor offered her a choice between accepting them and drinking a cup of poison. She drank the cup at once, and it turned out to hold only vinegar. The emperor gave up, and jealousy came to be called eating vinegar.
story.source: a popular tale about the Tang chancellor Fang Xuanling and his wife

use.how: A verb-object phrase: 吃醋, 爱吃醋, 吃谁的醋, 吃什么醋. Said, often teasingly, of jealousy within a couple or a romance.

near.diff: 眼红 is envy of what others have, such as money or success; 吃醋 is jealousy about someone you love paying attention to another.
嫉妒 is the general word for jealousy or envy of any kind; 吃醋 is the light, colloquial word for romantic jealousy.

cue: Your girlfriend frowns every time a female colleague texts you and keeps asking who she is. What is going on with her?

ctx.s: 你是不是在{吃醋}？怎么不说话了？
ctx.en: Are you jealous? Why have you gone quiet?

ctx.s: 我只是跟女同事说了几句话，你{吃什么醋}啊？
ctx.en: I only said a few words to a female colleague. What are you jealous about?

ctx.s: 他女朋友很爱{吃醋}，不让他跟别的女生聊天。
ctx.en: His girlfriend gets jealous easily and won't let him chat with other girls.

ctx.s: 看到男朋友给别的女生点赞，她有点儿{吃醋}了。
ctx.en: Seeing her boyfriend like another girl's posts, she got a little jealous.

ctx.s: 别{吃他的醋}了，他只是我的老同学。
ctx.en: Don't be jealous of him, he's just an old classmate of mine.

ctx.s: 丈夫跟前女友吃了顿饭，她{吃了好几天的醋}。
ctx.en: Her husband had a meal with his ex-girlfriend, and she was jealous for days.

bad.s: 看到邻居买了新车，我很{吃醋}。
bad.en: (meant: seeing the neighbours buy a new car, I was very envious)
bad.why: It is jealousy in love, not envy of someone's possessions; for that say yan hong or xian mu.

bad.s: 我真{吃醋}你，你男朋友那么帅！
bad.en: (meant: I'm so jealous of you, your boyfriend is so handsome!)
bad.why: A calque of English 'jealous of you' meaning envy; it takes no object like this, and envy of someone's luck is xian mu.

mean: to leave one's job to work for another employer
lit: to jump to another trough, like a horse leaving its own manger to feed at another

use.how: An intransitive verb-object phrase: 跳槽, 跳槽到某公司, 跳了两次槽. Said of employees moving to another employer, usually for better pay or prospects.

near.diff: 辞职 is simply resigning, with nothing said about what comes next; 跳槽 means moving on to work somewhere else.
炒鱿鱼 is being fired by the employer; 跳槽 is leaving by one's own choice for a new job.

cue: A rival company offers your best engineer a higher salary, and next month she starts working for them. What has she done?

ctx.s: 他去年{跳槽}到了一家外企。
ctx.en: Last year he moved to a job at a foreign company.

ctx.s: 你为什么想{跳槽}？现在的公司不好吗？
ctx.en: Why do you want to change jobs? Is your current company no good?

ctx.s: 年轻人{跳槽}很常见，大多是为了更高的工资。
ctx.en: It's common for young people to switch employers, mostly for higher pay.

ctx.s: 她三年里{跳了两次槽}，现在已经是部门经理了。
ctx.en: She changed companies twice in three years and is now a department manager.

ctx.s: 公司待遇太低，好几个技术骨干都{跳槽}了。
ctx.en: The company pays too little, and several of its key engineers have left for other firms.

ctx.s: 面试官问：“你频繁{跳槽}的原因是什么？”
ctx.en: The interviewer asked: "Why have you changed employers so often?"

bad.s: 我太累了，所以{跳槽}回家休息一年。
bad.en: (meant: I was exhausted, so I quit my job to rest at home for a year)
bad.why: It means moving to another employer; leaving work to rest is ci zhi (resign).

bad.s: 他成绩特别好，从三年级{跳槽}到了五年级。
bad.en: (meant: his grades were so good that he skipped from third to fifth grade)
bad.why: It is only about changing jobs; skipping a grade at school is tiao ji.

mean: to dampen someone's enthusiasm with discouraging words
lit: to throw cold water over someone

use.how: A verb-object phrase, often 给某人泼冷水 or 泼了一盆冷水. Said of discouraging someone's plans, hopes or excitement.

near.diff: 唱反调 is deliberately taking the opposite position; 泼冷水 is deflating someone's hopes or excitement, even with good intentions.
说风凉话 is sneering from the sidelines at someone's trouble; 泼冷水 is discouraging a plan or hope before it starts.

cue: Your friend excitedly tells you she wants to open a café, and you immediately list every reason it will fail. What are you doing to her?

ctx.s: 孩子想学画画，你就别给他{泼冷水}了。
ctx.en: The child wants to learn to paint, so don't discourage him.

ctx.s: 看你这么兴奋，不是我{泼冷水}，这个计划真的太冒险了。
ctx.en: I can see you're excited, and I don't mean to dampen your spirits, but this plan really is too risky.

ctx.s: 我刚说想参加比赛，他就{泼冷水}，说我肯定不行。
ctx.en: As soon as I said I wanted to enter the contest, he poured cold water on it and said I'd never make it.

ctx.s: 大家正兴高采烈地讨论旅行，经理的一句话给大家{泼了一盆冷水}。
ctx.en: Everyone was happily discussing the trip when one remark from the manager killed the mood.

ctx.s: 第一次创业失败后，家人还不停地{泼冷水}，他心里很难受。
ctx.en: After his first business failed, his family kept discouraging him, and it hurt him deeply.

ctx.s: 对新员工的想法，我们应该多鼓励，少{泼冷水}。
ctx.en: We should encourage new employees' ideas more and discourage them less.

bad.s: 他上课迟到了，老师{泼冷水}批评了他一顿。
bad.en: (meant: he was late for class, and the teacher gave him a scolding)
bad.why: It means dampening hopes or enthusiasm, not scolding someone for a mistake; for that say pi ping (criticise).

bad.s: 朋友的鼓励给我{泼了冷水}，我更有信心了。
bad.en: (meant: my friend's encouragement boosted me and made me more confident)
bad.why: It means the opposite: discouraging someone. Encouragement is gei wo da qi (cheer me on).

mean: to take the blame for someone else's mistake
lit: to carry a soot-blackened cooking pot on one's back

use.how: A verb-object phrase, often 替某人背黑锅, 背了黑锅, 背这个黑锅. Said of an innocent person who is blamed, usually with sympathy or resentment.

near.diff: 甩锅 is what the guilty person does in pushing the blame away; 背黑锅 is what happens to the person who ends up carrying it.
替罪羊 is a noun for the person made to take the blame; 背黑锅 is the verb phrase for taking it.

cue: Your manager lost the contract, but in the meeting he said it was your fault, and you were the one who got the warning. What happened to you?

ctx.s: 明明是他弄坏的，凭什么让我{背黑锅}？
ctx.en: He was obviously the one who broke it, so why should I take the blame?

ctx.s: 我可不想替你{背这个黑锅}。
ctx.en: I'm certainly not going to take the blame for you on this one.

ctx.s: 项目出了问题，最后是新来的实习生{背了黑锅}。
ctx.en: When the project went wrong, the new intern ended up taking the blame.

ctx.s: 为了保护朋友，他主动{背了黑锅}。
ctx.en: To protect his friend, he took the blame himself.

ctx.s: 事故原因终于查清楚了，小李不用再{背黑锅}了。
ctx.en: The cause of the accident has finally been established, so Xiao Li no longer has to carry the blame.

ctx.s: 你放心，这件事我不会让你一个人{背黑锅}。
ctx.en: Don't worry, I won't let you take the blame for this alone.

bad.s: 他把自己的错误{背黑锅}给了同事。
bad.en: (meant: he pushed the blame for his own mistake onto a colleague)
bad.why: Pushing your own blame onto others is shuai guo; this idiom describes the innocent person who ends up blamed.

bad.s: 这次失败完全是我自己的错，我应该{背黑锅}。
bad.en: (meant: this failure was entirely my own fault, so I should take responsibility)
bad.why: It implies the blame is undeserved. For your own fault say cheng dan ze ren (take responsibility).
